newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.Africa's policy impotence - By C.Mason.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.Africa's policy impotence - By C.Mason.

text.p: By Carole Mason, group economist at Investec Bank Ltd
Current financial market angst reflects growing concern at the outright impotence of domestic economic policy.

In an environment where it often appears that the slightest hint of criticism of official policy is dismissed as being motivated out of self-interest or a lack of appreciation for the wider subtleties involved, the authorities, through continuing lip-service to reform, have moved some considerable way towards alienating the very constituency (i.e. the financial markets) they can least afford to cross.

Motivated by a considerable sense of concern that the global investment community will simply tire of South Africa's perpetual plea for patience, the following comments are offered in a spirit of constructive criticism and out of recognition that the "self-preservation" thrust of economic policy that might have been appropriate in the old South Africa is no longer valid in the new.
GOVERNMENT COMMENTS LIKELY TO DISCOURAGE INVESTORS

Recent comments by the authorities, which once again highlight their commitment to gradual structural reform (particularly in relation to exchange control removal), represent nothing less than an open invitation to all would-be investors to postpone investing in South Africa.

By indicating that exchange control removal will take another four to five years, the authorities have unwittingly sent a clear signal that investors should hold off making any investment in this country until such time as the rand has found its new, market-determined, level.

Although possibly intended to restore a degree of certainty to the policy environment in South Africa, these latest comments merely confirm what many had begun to suspect -- that policy prevarication in South Africa will continue to be the order of the day.

Since would-be emerging market economies are increasingly expected to earn their place in the global economy, government's incessant pleas for investor patience run the risk of completely alienating investor sentiment, both locally and abroad, with detrimental consequences for an already-weakening economy.
MARKETS CAN FORCE GOVERNMENT TO ACT ON WORSE TERMS

There must now be a very real danger that financial markets will force the issue of liberalisation, inevitably at terms considerably less favourable than if government had seized the initiative itself. In the process, the authorities will lose even more credibility.

Undboubtedly well-intentioned, government's dogged pursuit of gradualist reform and support of the beleagured currency has increased the costs inevitably associated with structural adjustment, at the expense, ultimately, of the tax-paying public, the unemployed and the poor.

Government's latest policy comments effectively encourage speculative activity against the rand. Given the possibility of further market turbulence, the question must be asked whether the monetary policy mandate of the authorities actually extends to increasing the burden on an already stretched tax-paying public? Simply put, why should the tax-paying public be forced to pay for the speculative excesses generated by policy indecisiveness and timidity on the part of the authorities?

Rather than pursue current loose policy, the essential thrust of which has been acknowledged as "a little bit of this and a little bit of that", government has little choice but to fast forward its plans for liberalisation of the economy, so that market certainty can be restored, substantively higher adjustment costs avoided and hitherto elusive higher growth realised.
FREEING CURRENCY, PRIVATISATION SHOULD BE PRIORITIES
As a matter of priority it should push ahead with plans for complete exchange control removal, privatisation, further reduction in tariffs and adoption of a more appropriate tax system.
The monetary authorities must immediately desist from their pointless attempt to put a floor under the value of the rand and, in the interest of the taxpayer, withdraw from the forward cover market.

Arguments that, in an environment of low foreign exchange reserves exchange controls cannot be lifted simply no longer wash. If anything, policy prevarication has intensified the risk of capital outflows because of a national undermining of confidence in the domestic currency.
CURRENCY DEPRECIATION BETTER SOON THAN LATE, DESPITE COSTS

While it is acknowledged that exchange control abolition may result in further rand depreciation, with implications for inflation, the probable costs associated with this will be lower if action is taken now.

While financial market reverbations might be expected to persist following any dramatic opening up of the economy, the expectation that eventual benefits will more than outweigh intitial costs must be effectively communicated by government to all those for whom the prospect of rapid structual reform remains a concern.

Short-term structural adjustment costs must inevitably be set against expectations of significant export growth, job creation and reduced imports, such that the balance of payments position materially improves.

Recourse should also be made to IMF assistance and other available credit lines, not because of the monetary amounts involved, which are largely insignificant, but because of the signal that this would send to investors about the seriousness of government intent to open up the economy to increase investor participation.
DECISIVE LEADERSHIP AND CREDIBLE PLAN IS NEEDED

Tough times call for tough, decisive leadership. In an environment fraught with uncertainty, government's apparent willingness to ride out current difficulties merely exacerbates the root cause of current tension.
The authorities now need to bite the bullet and embark on bold, dramatic action, designed to show both investors and the financial markets that they have got what it takes to stop the current rot.

A plan that is seen to be consistent, coherent and, more importantly, credible, will do much to restore badly-damaged investor confidence and prevent acute market nervousness from spilling over into the real economy. At the very least, a further rise in interest rates has to be avoided.

For as long as the authorities hold out on fundamental reform, South Africa seems destined to remain in the ranks of those countries with acknowledged but largely unrealised potential. In an environment where delayed implementations can only mean delayed results, the authorities have little real choice but to acknowledge that things have not gone according to plan and activate those policies that generate the medium-term gains to which everyone aspires.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters. Subheadings added by Reuters.)
